stage0.title: Stage 0: the R-style starting point
stage0.did: Used the data exactly as the R project did: all 3,755 rows including duplicates, original columns one-hot encoded, salary modelled in dollars, an untuned random forest and default boosting.
happened: Random forest: RMSE $48,832, R² 0.398
Boosting: RMSE $49,033, R² 0.393
Training-set fit of the same forest: R² 0.57, the kind of plot the R report showed.
stage0.why: Copies of the same row can land in both the training and the test fold, so the model is partly graded on rows it has already seen. These are the most optimistic scores in the project.
stage0.takeaway: Treat stage 0 as the claim to test, not as a result.

stage1.title: Stage 1: remove duplicate rows
stage1.did: Dropped the 1,172 exact duplicate rows (31%). Nothing else changed.
stage1.why: This is a correction, not an optimisation, so scores are expected to get worse. It restores an honest test: no row in a test fold has a twin in the training fold.
stage1.takeaway: The honest baseline is R² 0.39 ($52,356 RMSE). Every later number is measured against it; the RMSE rose by $3,524 at most.

stage2.title: Stage 2: model log-salary
stage2.did: Predicted log(salary) and converted back to dollars, so errors grow with pay instead of being dominated by the highest earners.
stage2.why: A log target usually helps linear and neural models. Tree models split on order, not scale, so they gain little, and converting back adds a small bias.
stage2.takeaway: Both tree families got slightly worse here. The transform is kept for the model search, where it helps the linear and neural models.

stage3.title: Stage 3: cleaning and features
stage3.did: Learned from the training folds only: collapsed job titles and locations with fewer than 10 rows, added job family, region and a level ordinal, and trimmed the top and bottom 1% of salaries when fitting (never when scoring).
stage3.why: Fewer, better-supported categories are easier to learn from, and trimming limits the pull of extreme salaries without making the test set easier.
stage3.takeaway: A modest gain ($271 for the forest, $1,066 for boosting).

stage4.title: Stage 4: hyperparameter tuning
stage4.did: Ran a randomised search over tree depth, learning rate, regularisation and similar settings inside each cross-validation fold (nested CV).
stage4.why: Nesting keeps the search from seeing the rows it is scored on, so the score is an honest estimate of what tuning delivers.
stage4.takeaway: Tuning helps both families by $569 and $714: real, but small beside the noise in the data.

stage5.title: Stage 5: the best model
stage5.did: Compared ten model families under the same protocol; the lowest-error model is Stacking.
happened: Stacking: RMSE $51,366, MAE $36,798, R² 0.411
5 of 18 configurations are statistically tied with it, spanning only $146 of RMSE.
stage5.why: People with an identical profile (same title, level, location, company size, employment type, year and remote ratio) differ in salary by about 30%. A model that sees only these columns cannot beat the average of such a group.
stage5.takeaway: The ceiling is the data, not the algorithm. More modelling will not move the plot onto the diagonal; more information (skills, industry, tenure) might.

arena.title: The model arena
arena.did: Ran ridge, KNN, random forest, extra trees, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, a small neural net and a stacking blend, each at defaults and tuned, under one protocol (5-fold cross-validation repeated 3 times). CatBoost was evaluated at default settings only; its tuning run was stopped to save about 25 minutes.
happened: Lowest error: Stacking at $51,366 RMSE.
5 of 18 configurations are statistically tied with it, spanning $146 (0.3%).
Tuning moved the typical model by $125; the biggest gain was MLP at $1,692. 2 of 7 tuned models scored worse than their defaults on held-out folds.
arena.why: Each model is compared with the winner fold by fold, and a gap smaller than its corrected standard error counts as a tie. That separates real differences from fold-to-fold noise.
arena.takeaway: 8 of 10 model families land within 1% of the best; only Extra trees, KNN fall clearly behind. The choice of model barely matters here.

decision.title: The decision
decision.did: A rule fixed before the results: 1) the accuracy winner has the lowest mean RMSE; 2) models whose gap to the winner is smaller than its standard error are tied; 3) among tied models pick the simplest; 4) for the range-based product pick the simplest tied model with native quantile output.
happened: Accuracy winner: Stacking.
Parsimonious pick: XGBoost, $12 behind the winner and far simpler.
Near-tie: ridge regression misses the cutoff by under a dollar (gap $75, standard error $75), is 0.15% behind the best and is the most interpretable model.
Product pick by the rule: XGBoost. On the 10-90% range LightGBM has the lowest pinball loss ($8,555); the web app uses LightGBM quantile models (coverage 76.9%, median width $115,402).
decision.why: The rule did not score interval quality, and the four quantile models differ by only 1.2% on it, so the app keeps LightGBM as a deliberate, stated exception to the rule's XGBoost pick.
decision.takeaway: No model is clearly better. Use the simplest one for accuracy, a quantile boosting model for ranges, and spend effort on better data.

insights.title: What the business can do with this
insights.did: Fitted a log-salary linear model with 300 bootstrap resamples to put each factor in percent, built pay bands by role family, level and market, and checked how often real salaries fell inside the model's 80% range, by segment.
happened: Location is the dominant lever: the same role pays about 35% less in the UK, 51% less elsewhere in Europe and 81% less in India than in the US.
Seniority compounds: mid +34%, senior +73%, executive +115% versus entry level.
Role matters less: analysts earn 19% less than engineers; ML/AI roles +14% and leadership +19%.
Fully remote work shows no reliable pay difference (-1%, interval spans zero). Small companies pay 18% less than medium ones.
Pay trends up about +7% a year across 2020-2023.
insights.why: Raw accuracy is modest (R² about 0.4), so the value is benchmarking, not single-number prediction. Coverage is 77.5% overall with a median range of $115,245, and weakest for Rest of world (70%, n=116), IN (74%, n=57), ML/AI (74%, n=386), CA (75%, n=83), Entry (75%, n=270).
insights.takeaway: Use the bands to frame pay conversations, and read thin segments (small n) as a prompt for more data rather than a conclusion.

decisions.q: Set or review a pay band
decisions.a: Start from the 25-75% band for the role family, level and market, then adjust for company size (about -18% for small firms).
decisions.c: High where n is large (US engineers, scientists, analysts)

decisions.a: Enter the profile in the estimator. Treat the 10-90% range as plausible and an offer below it as a retention or fairness flag.
Location is the biggest cost driver. The data quantifies the gap; it cannot judge output or quality.
decisions.c: High for UK, Europe, India; low for thin locations

decisions.a: Remote work shows no reliable salary penalty or premium (-1%), so remote alone does not change what you must pay.
Plan for about +34% from entry to mid and +73% from entry to senior.
About +7% a year in this sample.
decisions.c: Low: four years of survey data

estimator.title: How to read an estimate
estimator.did: Three quantile models predict the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of salary for the profile you enter. A peer range shows what comparable people actually reported.
happened: The 10-90% range covered 76.9% of held-out salaries (target 80%), with a median width of $115,402.
estimator.why: Titles, levels and locations explain only about 40% of salary variance, so any honest estimate has to be wide. Categories with fewer than 5 rows trigger a warning because the model has almost nothing to learn from.
estimator.takeaway: Treat the range as the answer and the middle tick as its most likely value.

explorer.title: Explore the data
explorer.did: Group and filter the 2,583 unique rows by any field. Bars show the 25th-75th percentile range and the median.
explorer.why: Small groups are hidden by default (minimum 10 rows) because their medians move a lot with one or two people.
explorer.takeaway: Click a row to filter to it.

limits.title: Limits to state out loud
happened: Self-reported survey data, 2020-2023, USD. It is not a payroll dataset and it is not current.
Seven columns only: no skills, tenure, industry, company name or education, which is why R² stops near 0.4.
Associations, not causes: location effects bundle cost of living, taxes and local labour markets.
Thin segments should not drive decisions.
A range is not an offer: use the model to frame a conversation, not to set an individual's pay.

hero.title: A salary is a range, not a number
hero.did: A study of 2,583 data-science salaries, rebuilt from a class project: honest evaluation, ten models, and what a business can actually do with the result.
